title: Out-of-Pocket Health Spending and Neonatal Mortality in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: Between- and Within-Country Evidence from 124 Countries, 2010–2021
content: Background: Out-of-pocket (OOP) payments remain a major share of health financing in many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and can deter women from using maternal and newborn care. Whether countries that rely more heavily on OOP payments have higher neonatal mortality, and whether changes in that reliance track changes in mortality, has not been examined across a recent, broad panel of LMICs. Methods: We conducted an ecological panel analysis of 124 LMICs (21 low-, 46 lower-middle- and 57 upper-middle-income) observed annually from 2010 to 2021 (1,481 country-years), using World Development Indicators data. The exposure was OOP spending as a share of current health expenditure; the primary outcome was the log neonatal mortality rate (NMR). We fitted pooled regression models with year effects and country-clustered standard errors, adjusting for health expenditure per capita, GDP per capita, urbanisation, fertility and income group, and two-way (country and year) fixed-effects models to estimate within-country associations. Secondary analyses examined maternal mortality, skilled birth attendance and heterogeneity by income group. Results: Median OOP share fell from 37.5% in 2010 to 32.5% in 2021, yet 50 of 124 countries still financed more than 40% of health spending out of pocket in 2021. In fully adjusted pooled models, each 10-percentage-point higher OOP share was associated with 4.1% higher NMR (95% CI 0.3 to 8.1). In two-way fixed-effects models, within-country changes in OOP share were not associated with NMR (−0.4%; 95% CI −2.5 to 1.7), a null finding that held across pre-pandemic, lagged and education-adjusted specifications. Higher OOP share was associated with lower skilled birth attendance (−1.9 percentage points per 10-point higher share; 95% CI −3.2 to −0.6), and adjusting for skilled birth attendance attenuated the OOP–NMR association by about 31%. No association was found with maternal mortality. Conclusions: Across LMICs, heavier reliance on OOP payments is a structural marker of higher neonatal mortality, partly through lower use of skilled birth care, but the modest year-to-year changes seen within countries over 2010–2021 did not track neonatal mortality. Sustained shifts toward prepaid, pooled financing and protection of the full cost of childbirth, rather than incremental changes, may be needed to influence newborn survival.
